title: Muslim-American institutional presence grows while public suspicion, discrimination, and partisan polarization persist
source_unit: Pew Research Center data essay with FBI Uniform Crime Reporting and mosque-count context

observations.period: May 4-17, 2026; public judgments about Muslim Americans

denominator.unit: percent of US adults in Pew survey

less_patriotic.unit: percent saying Muslims are less patriotic than other Americans

observations.method: Pew survey of US adults; neutral/unsure and no-answer categories are retained in the source but not shown in the headline contrasts.
observations.uncertainty: These are public judgments, not validated measures of national impact, patriotism, or policy conduct; subgroup sample and item wording details remain source-specific.
observations.subgroup: US adults; Muslim Americans as the judged group
observations.counterinterpretation: A negative judgment can reflect stereotype, political framing, personal experience, or other beliefs; the survey does not identify the mechanism.

observations.period: March 2002 and January 2026; public association of Islam with violence

denominator.unit: percent of US adults in comparable Pew survey items; historical mode changes apply

total_2002.unit: percent saying Islam is more likely than other religions to encourage violence

observations.method: Pew historical survey series; 2002-2015 telephone surveys and 2016-2026 American Trends Panel surveys, with a documented wording note for 2021.
observations.uncertainty: Mode, wording, political context, and survey composition complicate level comparisons; no causal media, party, or event mechanism is identified.
observations.counterinterpretation: The change may reflect multiple political, security, media, and social factors rather than a single post-9/11 trajectory.

observations.period: 2026; Muslim-American experiences of discrimination, unfair media portrayal, and support

denominator.unit: percent of US Muslim adults in Pew American Trends Panel and supplemental panels

a_lot_of_discrimination.unit: percent saying there is a lot of discrimination against Muslims

unfair_media_portrayal.unit: percent saying media portrayals are unfair

received_religion_based_support.unit: percent saying someone expressed support in past year because of their religion

observations.method: Pew 2026 American Trends Panel data supplemented by three nationally representative panels; source reports measures separately.
observations.uncertainty: The items measure perceived or recalled experience and are not a complete incident prevalence rate; subgroup and question wording details remain source-specific.
observations.counterinterpretation: Support and discrimination can coexist across people, settings, and time; the measures do not imply a uniform Muslim-American experience.

denominator.unit: reported incidents in participating law-enforcement agencies; not a population prevalence denominator

observations.method: FBI Uniform Crime Reporting Program hate-crime statistics as reproduced by Pew; category is anti-Islamic and excludes incidents with multiple bias motivations.
observations.uncertainty: Participation, reporting, category definitions, and the 2021 transition to NIBRS changed over time; counts are not total victimization or discrimination prevalence.
observations.subgroup: Reported incidents motivated by anti-Islamic bias
observations.counterinterpretation: Changes can reflect reporting and collection systems as well as underlying incidents.

observations.period: 2000-2026; Muslim population, mosque counts, and political representation context

denominator.unit: source-specific population estimates, mosque counts, and officeholder counts; not one common denominator

observations.method: Pew population estimates combine survey and Census information; mosque counts come from the Cooperative Congregational Studies Partnership; representation is contextual reporting.
observations.uncertainty: These measures have different units, dates, definitions, and estimation methods; they should not be pooled into an institutional-capacity index.
observations.counterinterpretation: Growth and officeholding do not establish equal access, safety, influence, policy success, or reduced discrimination.

related_sources.claim: The Latino mobility layer provides a neighboring migration, belonging, and cultural-meaning comparison.
The press-legitimacy layer provides a separate media-power and institutional-criticism context.

boundary: This record measures public attitudes, reported Muslim-American experiences, reported anti-Islamic hate-crime incidents, institutional presence, and political visibility. It does not establish causal effects of 9/11, party messaging, media, migration, mosque growth, individual voting, consumer behavior, service access, or total discrimination prevalence.
